_comment: #123 (RULED David 2026-08-20, EXTEND THE SIDECAR) — the ONE declaration of the runner-identity
keys benchd adds to benchmark-integrity.*.json on top of the reference's nine.
WHY A FILE. The roster had four independent encodings — two shell scripts, a Rust test vector,
and the IntegritySidecar struct's field order — and nothing tied them together, so a field added
in one place could pass every gate while the live parity legs silently stopped enforcing it.
Now:
scripts/facade-leg.sh, scripts/official-parity.sh   read `keys` from here with jq
crates/benchctl/src/main.rs (superset test)         include_str!s this file and asserts the
struct's emitted surplus SET equals it
which leaves the struct's field ORDER as the only thing the Rust test still states in its own
words — and that is a claim about ordering, which this file deliberately does not make.
SORTED, because both consumers compare it against `jq 'keys'` output, which is sorted. The Rust
side sorts its emitted surplus before comparing; the emitted ORDER is the struct's declaration
order and is asserted separately.
The live legs require this set EXACTLY — every key present, none extra. An empty surplus is a
FAIL, not a pass: a benchd that dropped the runner block is the precise regression #123 exists
to prevent.
candidate_executable_resolution (#132/F3) says whether candidate_executable is a canonical path
with a real digest or a path benchd could not resolve/read, recorded verbatim with an empty one.
It exists so an empty candidate_executable_sha256 is never ambiguous.
SORTEDNESS IS ENFORCED, not just documented: the Rust superset test asserts this array equals
its own sort (#132/F6). Both consumers compare it against `jq 'keys'` output, which is sorted, so
an unsorted edit here would break the live legs at a distance rather than here.
